**What this explains.** Before every edit, the [hold gate](hold-gate.qmd)
asks whether a set of contacts can hold the box against gravity. This page
derives the answer from first principles in two stages. First an **exact
test** that works in the plane: it turns the question into membership in a
cone in three dimensions and decides it with a *witness*, a *certificate*
and a *margin*. Then the **linear programs (LPs)** that answer the same
question in any dimension, with limits on the manipulator's force and
margins against a set of disturbances. The LPs are the gate today; the
exact test is its cross-check. You need Coulomb friction and a little
linear algebra. The code is in `cmg/src/cmg/physics/planar_hold.py`
(`cone_test`) and `hold_lp.py` on the branch `master`.

## 1. The question

A rigid box rests in the x–z plane on some contacts. Each contact pushes on
the box with a force that Coulomb friction confines to a cone. The box is
**supported** if some choice of admissible contact forces cancels gravity
exactly: the net force *and* the net moment. That is statics only: no
dynamics and no time.

## 2. From forces to one cone

**Friction cones have two edges.** At a contact with inward normal $n$,
tangent $t$ and friction coefficient $\mu$, the admissible forces are those
with $|f\cdot t| \le \mu\, f\cdot n$. In the plane that set is spanned by its
two edge rays:
$$
f = \lambda_+\,(n+\mu t) + \lambda_-\,(n-\mu t), \qquad \lambda_\pm \ge 0 .
$$

**A segment contact acts through its endpoints.** A contact set can be a
segment $[p_0,p_1]$ (an edge lying on the floor) with the same $n$ and $\mu$
along it. A force $f$ applied at $p = s\,p_0 + (1-s)\,p_1$ has the same
force and moment as $s f$ at $p_0$ plus $(1-s) f$ at $p_1$, because the
moment $(p-c)\times f$ is linear in $p$. So two points per contact suffice.
A point contact is the case $p_0 = p_1$.

**Wrenches.** Write each ray $r$ at each endpoint $p$ as a *wrench*: force
and moment about the center of mass $c$, made dimensionless,
$$
w = \Big(r_x,\; r_z,\; \tfrac{(p-c)\times r}{\ell}\Big) \in \R^3,
\qquad (p-c)\times r = (p-c)_z\, r_x - (p-c)_x\, r_z ,
$$
with forces in units of the weight $mg$ and moments in units of $mg\,\ell$,
where $\ell = a/2$ is the box's half-size. Gravity applies the wrench
$(0,-1,0)$ about the center of mass, so the contacts must supply
$$
\text{need} = (0,\, 1,\, 0).
$$

**The question becomes geometry.** Let $w_1,\dots,w_k$ be all the ray
wrenches (at most 4 contacts × 2 endpoints × 2 rays = 16). Then
$$
\boxed{\ \text{supported} \iff \text{need} \in C = \Big\{\textstyle\sum_i \lambda_i w_i : \lambda_i \ge 0\Big\}\ }
$$
where $C$ is the convex cone the generators span.

**Running example.** A square box flat on the floor, $\mu = 0.2$, touching at
its two bottom corners A (left) and B (right). In units of $\ell$, the corners
sit at $(\mp1,-1)$ from the center of mass. The four generators are:

| Ray | Force $(f_x, f_z)$ | Moment / ℓ | Wrench $w$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| A₊ | (+0.2, 1) | +0.8 | (0.2, 1, 0.8) |
| A₋ | (−0.2, 1) | +1.2 | (−0.2, 1, 1.2) |
| B₊ | (+0.2, 1) | −1.2 | (0.2, 1, −1.2) |
| B₋ | (−0.2, 1) | −0.8 | (−0.2, 1, −0.8) |

## 3. Seeing the cone

A cone in $\R^3$ is hard to draw, but when every generator pushes upward
($f_z > 0$) it is fixed by where its rays cross the plane $f_z = 1$. Each
generator becomes a point $(f_x/f_z,\ \tau/f_z)$, the cone becomes the convex
polygon of those points, and need becomes the origin. *Supported* then
means *the origin lies in the polygon*.

![Top: the box on both bottom corners (a) and on corner A alone (b), with each corner's friction cone. Bottom: the same two cones sliced at f<sub>z</sub> = 1. (c) The origin (need) lies inside the parallelogram, at the midpoint of A₊ and B₋: half the weight along each of those rays holds the box. (d) Corner A's two rays span a flat cone, and the plane through them separates the cone from need. Produced by `scripts/bg_cone_test.py`, which runs `cone_test` on both cases.](media/bg_cone_slice.svg){.lightbox}

The slice is only a picture. A disk pushing sideways can have $f_z \le 0$,
and every test below works in $\R^3$.

---

**Part I: the exact test.** Sections 4–8 decide support by enumeration, in the plane.

## 4. "Yes", with a witness: Carathéodory

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Carathéodory's theorem (conic form).** If $x \in \operatorname{cone}\{w_1,\dots,w_k\} \subset \R^d$, then $x$ is a nonnegative combination of at most $d$ *linearly independent* generators.
:::

*Why.* Suppose $x = \sum_i \lambda_i w_i$ with $\lambda > 0$ on generators
that are linearly dependent, so $\sum_i \alpha_i w_i = 0$ for some
$\alpha \ne 0$, which we may take to have a positive entry. Replace $\lambda$
by $\lambda - s\alpha$ and increase $s$ until the first coefficient hits
zero. The sum still equals $x$, the coefficients stay nonnegative, and one
generator has dropped out. Repeat until the generators are independent;
there are at most $d$ of them.

*Algorithm.* Here $d = 3$, so the test solves every subset of 1, 2 and 3
generators: $16 + 120 + 560 = 696$ tiny systems (a projection, a 2×2
system, Cramer's rule). A subset whose coefficients are $\ge 0$ and that
reproduces need is a **witness**: actual contact forces that hold the box.

*Example.* $\tfrac12 w_{A_+} + \tfrac12 w_{B_-} = (0, 1, 0)$: half the weight
through each corner, both forces leaning slightly inward (panels a, c).

## 5. "No", with a certificate: Farkas

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Farkas's lemma (cone form).** $x \notin \operatorname{cone}\{w_i\}$ if and only if some $y$ has $y\cdot w_i \ge 0$ for every $i$ and $y \cdot x < 0$.
:::

Geometrically, $y$ is the normal of a plane through the origin with every
generator on one side and need strictly on the other. Such a $y$ is a
**certificate**: anyone can check the $k+1$ inequalities.

*Which $y$ to try.* A full-dimensional polyhedral cone is the intersection
of the half-spaces of its facets, and each facet contains at least two
independent generators. So the normals $\pm\, w_i \times w_j$ of the planes
through two generators contain a certificate. Flat cones and single rays
need a few more candidates ($\pm w_i$, the negated part of need
perpendicular to $w_i$, normals of planes containing one generator, and
$-\text{need}$): 385 candidates for 16 generators in all.

*Example.* On corner A alone the generators $w_{A_\pm}$ span a flat cone.
The plane through both has normal $y = (1,-1,1)/\sqrt3$, with
$y\cdot w_{A_\pm} = 0$ and $y\cdot \text{need} = -0.577 < 0$: certified
unsupported (panel d). Physically, every force at A has a moment about the
center of mass unless it points straight at it, which is outside A's
friction cone.

## 6. How much: the margin is a signed distance

The test also returns
$$
m \;=\; \min_{y \text{ supporting},\ \|y\| = 1}\; y\cdot \text{need},
$$
the minimum over every candidate $y$ with all generators on its side.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Claim.** $m$ is the signed Euclidean distance from need to the boundary of $C$: inside $C$ the distance to the boundary, outside minus the distance to $C$, and $0$ when need lies on a flat cone.
:::

*Inside.* $C$ is the intersection of its facet half-spaces
$\{x : y_f\cdot x \ge 0\}$. A ball of radius $\rho$ around need fits in $C$
exactly when $\rho \le y_f\cdot\text{need}$ for every facet, so the
distance to the boundary is $\min_f y_f\cdot\text{need}$; any other
supporting plane bounds a larger half-space and gives a larger value.

*Outside.* The nearest point of $C$ lies inside a two-dimensional face, on
a generator's ray, or at the apex. The unit vector from need toward it is
then that face's normal, the negated perpendicular part of need, or
$-\text{need}$; all are candidates and support $C$. By duality,
$\operatorname{dist}(x, C) = \max\{-y\cdot x : y \text{ supporting},\ \|y\|\le1\}$.

*Checked.* On random cones the margin agrees with minus the NNLS distance
outside (to 3·10⁻⁶) and with the shortest exit along hundreds of
directions inside (to 4·10⁻⁷); this is a test in the suite.

The flat box has four facets:

| Facet | Through | Normal y | y · need | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sliding (friction toward +x) | A₊, B₊ | (−0.981, 0.196, 0) | **0.196** | friction gives out |
| Sliding (friction toward −x) | A₋, B₋ | (0.981, 0.196, 0) | **0.196** | friction gives out |
| Tipping about A | A₊, A₋ | (−1, 1, −1)/√3 | 0.577 | B lifts off |
| Tipping about B | B₊, B₋ | (1, 1, 1)/√3 | 0.577 | A lifts off |

So $m = \mu/\sqrt{1+\mu^2} = 0.196$, and sliding binds first. A purely
sideways push of up to $\mu\,mg = 0.2\,mg$ is absorbed; the *worst*
direction also lifts the box a little, which unloads friction, hence 0.196.
The tipping value does not depend on $\mu$, so with $\mu > 1/\sqrt2$ tipping
binds: $m = \min(\mu/\sqrt{1+\mu^2},\ 1/\sqrt3)$. For corner A alone,
$m = -0.636$: need lies 0.636 from the cone. The certificate of §5 gave
−0.577: any certificate proves "no", but only the nearest one measures the
gap. The distance mixes forces and moments, so it depends on $\ell$; the
yes/no answer does not.

## 7. Robustness comes cheaply

- **Friction.** A smaller $\mu$ narrows every cone, so for an interval of
  $\mu$ the worst case is its lower end.
- **Mass and center of mass** enter only through need, which is linear in
  $(m,\ m c)$. Over a box of masses and centers the needs form a polytope,
  membership in a convex cone holds over a polytope iff it holds at its
  corners, and the margin's worst case is also at a corner.

## 8. Where the exact test stops

The enumeration has two limits.

- **Force limits.** The disk's push is bounded by its motors. With bounded
  forces the supportable wrenches are no longer a cone, and the candidate
  planes of §5 no longer describe them. Without limits, the disk's
  unbounded push often makes $C$ all of $\R^3$, and the margin is infinite.
- **Three dimensions.** A spatial wrench has 6 components, so Carathéodory
  needs subsets of up to 6 generators. With 4 contacts × 4 points × 8 rays
  of a pyramidal friction cone (128 generators), that is
  $\binom{128}{6} \approx 5.4\times10^{9}$ subsets.

Both limits disappear when the same question is posed as linear programs.

---

**Part II: the linear programs.** Sections 9–14 answer the same question in any dimension, with force limits and margins.

## 9. One backbone, any dimension

The LPs take four pieces of data:

| Data | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $W \in \R^{d\times k}$ | generators: one column per friction-cone edge at each support point, as a wrench |
| $\text{need} \in \R^d$ | the wrench the contacts must supply |
| $B\,\lambda \le f_{\max}$ (optional) | force limits |
| $u_1, \dots, u_J$ (optional) | disturbance directions for the margin |

The unknowns are the edge weights $\lambda \ge 0$. Only the builder of $W$
and need knows the dimension: planar wrenches have $d = 3$ and exactly two
edges per friction cone; spatial ones have $d = 6$ and an inner pyramid of
$m$ edges $n + \mu(\cos\theta_j t_1 + \sin\theta_j t_2)$ at the vertices of
each contact polygon. The pyramid lies inside the true cone, so it can only
reject wrongly, never accept, and 8 edges keep at least $\cos(\pi/8) = 92\%$
of the friction in every direction.

## 10. LP-1: feasibility, with a witness and a certificate

"Find $\lambda \ge 0$ with $W\lambda = \text{need}$" has no solution exactly
when the answer is no, and some solvers then report nothing more. Adding
slack that pays for any mismatch makes it always solvable:
$$
\text{LP-1:}\qquad \delta \;=\; \min_{\lambda,\, s^+,\, s^- \,\ge\, 0}\; \mathbf 1^\top s^+ + \mathbf 1^\top s^-
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad W\lambda + s^+ - s^- = \text{need}.
$$

- $\lambda = 0$ with $s^\pm$ the positive and negative parts of need is
  feasible, and $\delta \ge 0$.
- $\delta = \min_{\lambda \ge 0}\|W\lambda - \text{need}\|_1$, the ℓ₁
  distance from need to $C$; $\delta = 0$ means supported.
- **Yes comes with a witness.** The simplex method returns a *basic*
  optimal solution with at most $d$ nonzero variables: Carathéodory's
  theorem again, now produced by the solver.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Dual of LP-1.** $\displaystyle \delta = \max_{y}\ \text{need}^\top y \quad\text{s.t.}\quad W^\top y \le 0,\ \ -\mathbf 1 \le y \le \mathbf 1.$
:::

**No comes with a certificate.** If $\delta > 0$, then $z = -y$ has
$z\cdot w_i \ge 0$ for every generator and $z\cdot\text{need} < 0$: the
Farkas certificate of §5, at no extra cost.

*Example.* Both corners: $\delta = 0$ with witness
$\lambda_{A_+} = \lambda_{B_-} = \tfrac12$, as in §4. Corner A alone:
$\delta = 1.0$ with dual $y = (-1, 1, -1)$, so $z = (1, -1, 1)$: the
certificate of §5, unscaled.

## 11. LP-2: the margin, as exit distances

A Euclidean ball is not a polytope, so the margin of §6 is not an LP. A
polytope of disturbances is. For a direction $u$, the **exit distance** is
how far need can move along $u$ before leaving the supportable set:
$$
\text{LP-2:}\qquad t(u) \;=\; \max_{\lambda \ge 0,\ 0 \le t \le T}\; t
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad W\lambda = \text{need} + t\,u ,
$$
capped at $T = 10$ where the set never ends in that direction.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Claim (set inclusion).** For a convex polytope $D$ of disturbances, the largest $r$ with $\text{need} + rD$ supported is $\min_j t(d_j)$ over the corners $d_j$ of $D$.
:::

*Why.* $\text{need} + rD$ is the convex hull of its corners, so a convex
set contains it exactly when it contains the corners; along each corner's
direction the supportable points form an interval $[0, t(d_j)]$.

The gate uses $D$ = the ℓ₁ unit ball, whose corners are the pure
disturbances $\pm e_i$ (a push along x, a lift, a twist). With LP-1 this
gives a **signed ℓ₁ margin**: $\min_i t(\pm e_i)$ inside and $-\delta$
outside. It is always within a factor $\sqrt3$ of the Euclidean margin of
§6 ($\sqrt6$ in 3D).

![Exit distances of the flat box along the six pure directions, from LP-2. (a) On two corners: the margin is the sideways push, 0.2·mg = μ·mg. Pushing down (+f<sub>z</sub>) never breaks support; lifting by the full weight (−f<sub>z</sub>) and twisting by mg·ℓ (±τ) do. (b) With the disk pushing on the left face at the height of the center of mass, and its normal force limited to 0.5·mg: the +f<sub>x</sub> exit rises to 0.72, but the margin stays 0.2, because the disk pushes only one way. From `scripts/bg_hold_lp.py` (HiGHS, float64).](media/bg_lp_exits.svg){.lightbox}

The flat box's ℓ₁ margin is 0.2, exactly μ: the smallest pure push that
breaks support. Its Euclidean margin was 0.196, because the worst Euclidean
direction mixes a push with a slight lift.

## 12. LP-3: force limits

Every edge has unit normal component, so a contact's normal force is the
sum of its edge weights, and a limit is one more row. The gate uses the
simulator's motors instead: held still, the disk's two slide motors (±1 N
each, read from the MuJoCo model) must supply its push on the box plus its
own weight, $u = A(F - f_M)$, which gives two rows per motor. The feasible
wrenches are then the environment's cone plus a polytope from the disk, and
directions the disk helps have finite exits: in panel (b),
$t(+f_x) = 0.72 = 0.5$ from the disk plus $0.2 \times 1.1$ of floor
friction, since the disk's friction also presses the box onto the floor.
The dual gains one multiplier per row; the certificate stays a few
inequalities anyone can check.

## 13. Solving it inside JAX

The LPs are tiny and dense ($d = 3$ or $6$ rows, tens to a hundred-odd
columns), many are solved at once, and the interesting ones sit on the
support boundary, where they are degenerate.

| Method | Returns | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| **Simplex** | a vertex (witness with ≤ d generators) and the dual (certificate) | best: a handful of pivots, exact up to rounding |
| Interior point | an interior point; duals | workable; dense witness, delicate certificate near the boundary |
| First-order (PDHG, e.g. MPAX) | an approximate point | poor: slow near the boundary, and an early stop cannot certify "no". MPAX falsely rejected about 193 of 416 supported near-boundary cases |

**linrax** (a two-phase tableau simplex in JAX, pinned to 0.3.0) is the
solver; HiGHS (via SciPy, float64) checks every answer in the tests.
`hold_lp` replaces linrax's pivot loop at import with three changes: a cap
of 300 pivots per phase (under `vmap` one LP that never finishes hangs the
batch), Bland's leaving rule (linrax's rule let a 3D LP cycle), and a
corrected test for artificial rows (which had returned a slack of −1 as
"optimal" on the flat box). linrax returns no dual, so the dual is
recovered from the final basis by solving $B^\top y = c_B$.

**Float32.** All computations stay in float32. Four measures, each fixing
a failure the tests found:

1. the equality rows are rotated by a Householder reflection that makes
   every right-hand side positive (the planar need $(0,1,0)$ has two zero
   rows);
2. the primal is recomputed from the final basis rather than read off the
   tableau;
3. the pivot tolerance is $10^{-4}$ (at linrax's $10^{-6}$ it pivoted on
   noise: 19 wrong answers on 600 random LPs, none at $10^{-4}$);
4. exits are capped at $T = 10$, not $10^3$ (the large cap's coefficient fell
   to the pivot threshold and produced negative weights).

Every answer is then checked independently, with elementwise products (no
reduced-precision TF32 on GPUs): a witness by its residual, a certificate
by its signs, an exit by its weights. The gate's margin is a certified lower
bound: each exit's witness is checked by a residual bound with float32 rounding
accounted for, and the margin is the least of those bounds, so a solver error
can shrink the margin but not enlarge it. "Held" is certified only by a witness
with margin at least γ<sub>min</sub>, "not held" only by a Farkas certificate;
anything else is uncertain.

**Benchmark, before force limits** (record at commit `e29d96f`; 1,000 random
cases and 416 within 2 mm of disk height of the boundary; HiGHS reference;
float32):

| Device | Exact test, near boundary | LP, near boundary | ms per 256: exact / LP-1 / LP with margins |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU | 390 of 416 | 386 of 416 | 4.1 / 2.7 / 6.3 |
| GPU | 389 of 416 | 383 of 416 | 1.5 / 2.0 / 2.5 |

Both get all 1,000 random cases right; every other disagreement is a pose
reported uncertain and rejected (the safe direction), where a witness needs
weights of 60–190 times the box's weight, beyond what float32 can check.
The gate's own checks, with motor limits, are on
[the hold gate](hold-gate.qmd#accuracy).

**In 3D.** On a cube touched by up to four contacts (8-edge pyramids,
$d = 6$, up to 128 generators, 1,024 cases), nothing hangs, nothing is
certified wrongly, 763 of 768 random and 255 of 256 near-boundary cases
are right, and the rest are "uncertain" (safe) except one false acceptance
0.1% outside the boundary. The uncertain cases come from float32 rounding
over the longer pivot sequences; the cure would be rebuilding the tableau
from the final basis (*reinversion*). The 3D build is frozen; the project is
planar.

## 14. How the gate uses them

- **The gate** is LP-1 and LP-2 with the motor rows, on the edit's
  less-constrained end, at χ₀ and at the transition sweep's poses
  ([the hold gate](hold-gate.qmd#sweep)). It accepts when the certified
  margin is at least γ<sub>min</sub> = 10<sup>−5</sup>.
- **The margin** is set inclusion with the ℓ₁ ball; a scene can pass its
  own polytope $D$.
- **The exact test** (§4–6) stays as a cone-only cross-check.

| | Exact test (plane only) | LPs (any dimension) |
|---|---|---|
| Yes | witness, ≤ 3 generators | witness, ≤ d generators (basic solution) |
| No | Farkas plane from a candidate list | Farkas plane from the dual |
| Margin | signed Euclidean distance | signed ℓ₁ distance, or set inclusion of any polytope |
| Force limits | no | yes (rows) |
| 3D | no (about 5×10⁹ subsets) | yes (6 rows) |

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 1. What is the flat box's Euclidean margin with μ = 0.5, and what binds?
$0.5/\sqrt{1.25} = 0.447 < 1/\sqrt3 = 0.577$: sliding still binds.
`cone_test` returns 0.4472.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 2. Can a larger μ let corner A alone hold the flat box?
No. Every wrench a force at A can produce lies in one plane,
$\tau/\ell = f_z - f_x$ (arm $(-1,-1)$), whatever $\mu$ is. Need $= (0,1,0)$
gives $1 \ne 0$, so it is off that plane. A single point contact holds a body
only if the vertical through the center of mass passes through that point
and the vertical lies in its friction cone.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 3. Why does the exact test try planes through *two* generators, not three?
A plane through the origin in $\R^3$ is fixed by two independent directions.
Every facet of a 3D cone is such a plane and contains at least two
generators; three on one plane add nothing new.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 4. Why can LP-1 never report "infeasible"?
$\lambda = 0$ with $s^\pm$ equal to the positive and negative parts of need
satisfies every constraint, and the objective is at least 0. So the LP is
feasible and bounded, and the solver always ends with an optimal basis and
its dual.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 5. In 3D with an 8-edge pyramid, can the test accept a pose that real friction cannot hold?
No. The pyramid lies inside the true friction cone, so every force it allows
is a real force. The error is one-sided: it may reject a pose that needs
more than 92% of the available friction in an unlucky direction.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 6. In panel (b) of the exit figure, why does adding the disk not raise the margin?
The margin is the smallest exit. The disk can only push in +x, so it cannot
help resist a disturbance that needs −x force from the contacts; floor
friction alone sets $t(-f_x) = 0.2$. A second disk on the other face would.
:::

## Reproduce

```bash
cd ~/repos/research/c-gnn && git switch master && git pull && cd cmg
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv314/bin/python <website>/research/nonprehensile/planar-build/scripts/bg_cone_test.py <out dir>  # §2–6, cone figure
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv314/bin/python <website>/research/nonprehensile/planar-build/scripts/bg_hold_lp.py <out dir>    # §10–12, exit figure
# the benchmark of §13 is a record: bg_hold_lp_bench.py runs at commit e29d96f
```
